tier_reason: The peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) SOSD paper (Marcus et al.) benchmarks FAST against the STX B-Tree. Table 2 gives FAST 435.33 ns / 102.0 MB against BTree 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, and Sec. 4.5 states the 32x at 40 threads. It is not A: the benchmark code is public (learnedsystems/SOSD, benchmarks/benchmark_fast64.cc plus competitors/fast64_search.h, which wraps this repo as a submodule) and the CPU is named (Xeon Gold 6230), but neither the paper nor the SOSD README states a compiler or version.

corrections.workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn dataset (200M keys), comparing FAST against a tuned STX B-Tree. The Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn, which SOSD runs through this crate's create_fast32 path. The 64-bit results (Fig. 7 Pareto, Fig. 10, Fig. 16 multithreading) appear only as plots.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Table 2 (32-bit amzn, fastest variant of each structure): FAST 435.33 ns/lookup (102.0 MB) vs BTree 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB), about 1.1x lower latency (derived from page data). IBTree is 446.55 ns and plain binary search 741.69 ns. Separately, FAST had the highest relative multithreaded speedup of any structure tested: 32x throughput at 40 threads against its own single-thread run.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. From the code: SOSD's CMakeLists.txt adds -ffast-math -Wall -march=native (plus -fopenmp), and fast64's c/Makefile builds the AVX-512 lookup with gcc -O3 -march=native. The compiler used for the paper runs is unstated.
corrections.caveats: The single-thread margin over STX B-Tree in Table 2 is small (about 10%), and that table uses 32-bit keys, not 64-bit. The 32x claim is a self-relative multithreading speedup, not a multithreaded FAST-vs-BTree comparison, so do not read it as a 32x win over BTree. The fast lookup path is AVX-512 C code (build.rs checks for avx512f); machines without it get a slower safe Rust path. In the same paper FAST is slower than the learned indexes (RMI 180.90 ns, RS 266.58 ns, PGM 326.48 ns) and the hash tables, and it has one of the longest build times.

notes: Metadata checked and correct: GPL-3.0, 8 stars, last commit 2020-04-23, not a fork, not archived, so abandoned. SOSD pulls this repo in as the fast64 git submodule and uses it for both the FAST32 and FAST64 competitors, so the Table 2 FAST row does belong to this project. SOSD's older SSE competitors/fast.h is a separate class.

tier_reason: The SIGMOD'18 paper (Sec. 6.1-6.2, Fig. 8) compares HOT against the STX B+-Tree, ART and Masstree, and both quoted sentences appear verbatim. It names both CPUs and GCC 7.2 but no optimization flags. The repo's apps/benchmarks run only HOT, and the published index-microbench fork holds only the workload generator plus STX/ART wrappers, so no public harness reproduces the comparison. Not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.2 (stated in the paper). The paper gives no flags. The repo's CMakeLists.txt Release build (default USEAVX2=ON) uses -std=c++14 -march=native -mavx -mavx2 -mbmi2 -mlzcnt -O3 -DNDEBUG.
corrections.caveats: SIGMOD 2018 peer-reviewed paper. It states two CPU models and GCC 7.2 but no optimization flags, which caps it at Tier B. The 200% (3x) margin is workload E on the url data set only; workload C is at least 25%. ART inserts 50% faster than HOT on the integer data set. Needs AVX2/BMI2. The repo has had no pushes since 2018: treat it as a frozen academic artifact, not an actively developed library.

notes: Metadata checked and correct: ISC, 159 stars, last commit 2018-03-26, not a fork, not archived, so abandoned. The benchmark_url is a CMU course mirror of the SIGMOD'18 paper (DOI 10.1145/3183713.3196896); the text matches.

tier_reason: The AIDB@VLDB'21 extended abstract (peer-reviewed workshop) plots PLEX against BTree, ART, PGM, RMI, RS and CHT on the four 64-bit SOSD datasets (Fig. 3). The PLEX lookup-time curve sits well below BTree's on every dataset. It is not A: the text gives only the machine type (AWS m5zn.metal, 4.5 GHz turbo), not a CPU model, compiler or flags, and the repo's own bench_end_to_end.cc compares only against RadixSpline.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Graph-only. In Fig. 3 (size vs lookup time, 200M 64-bit keys) the PLEX curve lies at roughly 200-300 ns against BTree's roughly 500-900 ns and ART's roughly 400-600 ns on amzn and face (approximate, read from the plot). The text gives no ratio. It says 'PGM, ART, and BTree eventually lose performance as the index size is increased', and it notes that PLEX fixes RadixSpline's outlier problem on face and sits at a constant offset of about 25 ns from RMI on amzn and face. In the plot, RMI is the faster of the two.
corrections.workload: Four 64-bit SOSD real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki; 200M keys each). Build time vs size is compared against RMI, CHT, PGM and RadixSpline (Fig. 2). Lookup time vs size is compared against those plus ART and BTree (Fig. 3).
corrections.caveats: AIDB@VLDB 2021 workshop extended abstract, not a full research-track paper. The hardware is an AWS instance type with no CPU model, and the compiler and flags are not stated. The speedup evidence is only plots with no quoted number. PLEX does not beat RMI on lookup latency (RMI is about 25 ns faster on amzn and face).

notes: Metadata checked and correct: MIT, 16 stars, last commit 2022-06-30 (over 3 years ago, so abandoned), not a fork, not archived. TrieSpline also ships as a SOSD competitor (competitors/ts), which is presumably how Fig. 3's BTree/ART comparison was run. Plot values above are approximate visual readings, not printed numbers.
